blocks.content: docker ps lists containers. By default it only shows the ones that are currently running, which trips up a lot of people expecting to see everything.
Plain docker ps, with no flags, only lists containers that are actively running right now. A container you stopped five minutes ago will not show up here at all, even though it still exists on disk.

docker ps
# CONTAINER ID   IMAGE   STATUS         PORTS         NAMES
# a1b2c3d4       nginx   Up 2 minutes   0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp   web

code.content:
docker ps
# CONTAINER ID   IMAGE   STATUS         PORTS         NAMES
# a1b2c3d4       nginx   Up 2 minutes   0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp   web

codes.bash:
docker ps
# CONTAINER ID   IMAGE   STATUS         PORTS         NAMES
# a1b2c3d4       nginx   Up 2 minutes   0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp   web

blocks.content: Add -a (all) to see every container regardless of state, running, stopped, or exited with an error. This is usually the first thing to check when you expect a container to be running and it is not, it will show up here even when it has exited.

blocks.alt: The -a flag reveals stopped and exited containers too

blocks.content:
docker ps -a
# Now includes containers with STATUS "Exited (1) 5 minutes ago"

code.content:
docker ps -a
# Now includes containers with STATUS "Exited (1) 5 minutes ago"

codes.bash:
docker ps -a
# Now includes containers with STATUS "Exited (1) 5 minutes ago"

blocks.content: Each row of docker ps output has a consistent set of columns: the container ID (a short hash), the image it was started from, its current status, and any port mappings, enough to identify and reason about a container at a glance.

blocks.alt: A consistent set of columns, every time

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: docker ps only shows running containers unless you add -a, which is the most common gotcha for anyone new to it.
The output columns (ID, image, status, ports) are usually enough to identify exactly which container you are looking at.
